title: Viewport-adaptive tables & gesture-friendly controls for cost and rollout surfaces
creator: Ava Patel
description:
Goal: Create a resilient, low-friction responsive layer for cost tables, rollout timelines, and dashboard charts that works reliably across modern browsers (Chrome, Safari/iOS, Firefox, Edge) and on touch-driven devices. Scope covers: dense cost tables (sortable, column collapse), rollout timeline cards (horizontal scroll & small-screen collapse), chart canvases (fallbacks when WebGL/canvas perf degrades), modal stacking & focus handling, and gesture-friendly controls for dense surfaces.

Design constraints and assumptions:
- Performance budget: UI shell + responsive JS must not exceed 120KB gzipped for entry on list pages.
- Progressive enhancement: baseline HTML tables + minimal CSS must be usable without JS; enhanced features (sticky controls, drag-to-resize columns, continuous pan) layered on top.
- Accessibility-first: keyboard navigation, visible focus states, aria attributes for table region and modal traps.
- Cross-browser: explicit fallbacks for Safari canvas rendering and Firefox SVG quirks; touch momentum/overscroll behavior considered.

Deliverables:
- High-fidelity responsive Figma screens for 4 breakpoints (>=1200px, 900-1199px, 600-899px, <600px) for: cost table list, rollout timeline, per-route cost modal.
- Interactive prototype demonstrating: column collapse rules, sticky header behavior, timeline horizontal collapse, modal stacking & scroll lock.
- Implementation notes & review checklist for Engineering with edge-case matrix and swap mitigation strategies.

Trade-offs discussed in design: use of virtualization for very long cost tables reduces DOM but complicates sticky row/column behavior (decided to implement windowed virtualization with a sticky header shim and a lightweight intersection observer strategy to preserve keyboard focus and announce row changes). For charts, prefer canvas for performance but include an SVG fallback for Safari when canvas-backed WebGL path shows high CPU.
acceptance_criteria: All 4 breakpoints have Figma screens for cost table, rollout timeline, and per-route cost modal
Prototype demonstrates column collapse and touch swipe to reveal hidden columns on small screens
Engineering sign-off on virtualization approach and sticky header shim (GH PR linked in attachments)
Cross-browser test matrix shows no functional regression on Chrome, Safari (iOS & macOS), Firefox, Edge for listed interactions
Keyboard-only navigation through tables and modals passes accessibility audit (no keyboard traps, visible focus states)
comments: 2026-03-03 - Ava Patel: Initial concept sketches uploaded to Figma. Focus areas: how cost density impacts legibility and when to collapse columns vs horizontal scrolling.

2026-03-05 - Liam Chen: Explored two interaction patterns for small screens: (A) collapse-to-rows with a condensed meta row, (B) horizontal peek+swipe. Prototyped B; performs better on touch. Added prototype link.

2026-03-07 - Nora Williams (PM): Preference for pattern B — horizontal peek — because it preserves row context for billing reconciliations. Ask: include a quick keyboard-only reveal shortcut for power users.

2026-03-09 - Engineering review (Samir Gupta): Raised concerns about virtualization + sticky column; recommended a sticky shim (rendered DOM node at top) to maintain keyboard focus. Also flagged Safari canvas CPU spike; suggested fall back to SVG for small charts.

2026-03-11 - QA (Marta Ruiz): Started cross-browser smoke. Observed iOS Safari double-tap zoom interfering with horizontal swipe on timeline. Suggested touch-action: pan-x on timeline container and meta viewport tweak. Added to implementation notes.

2026-03-13 - Design review (Ava): Incorporated keyboard reveal shortcut (Shift+R) for collapsed columns and improved focus ring contrast. Updated prototype and PRD. Marking design deliverables ready for handoff to ENG.
2026-03-14 - Liam Chen: Preparing GH PR with the sticky header shim and intersection observer tests. Leaving TODOs for Firefox SVG quirks (stroke alignment) and Windows DPI tests.
